data.title: Maine senators push for Senate to take up House whale bill championed by lobster industry
data.description:
Maine’s two senators are urging the Senate Commerce Committee to take up and advance House-passed legislation that would extend a pause in rulemaking on protections for the right whales in an effort to safeguard the state’s lobster industry.

The House passed the Northeast Lobstermen Protection Act earlier this month after two Democrats, including sponsor Rep. Jared Golden (D-Maine), crossed party lines to back the procedural vote to allow the bill and other GOP priorities for a vote on the floor.

Sens. Susan Collins (R) and Angus King (I) said the regulations would have “effectively shut down the fishery,” in throwing their support behind the House bill.

“This pause is necessary to protect Maine’s lobster fishery, which is essential to the state’s economy and coastal communities. According to the Maine Lobstermen’s Association, the lobster industry supports an estimated $2 billion in annual economic activity and more than 17,500 jobs,” they wrote in a letter to the panel’s leadership.

In 2022, the pending whale regulations were punted to 2028 along with funding to further study whale migration patterns and the extent to which they overlay with lobstering territory.

King at the time called that legislation “a Christmas miracle for the lobster industry” and noted that a right whale had never become entangled in Maine lobster gear.

The bill Golden sponsored alongside Rep. Mike Lawler (R-N.Y.) would delay that again until 2035.

Collins previously called for passing the House bill to protect the lobster industry from “undue harm.”

Maine’s lobster industry is hopeful that more time to collect data will show improvements in the current population of less than 400 right whales as well as shifting migration patterns that may lie largely outside of the lobster fishing zone.

The whales have been killed in both ship strikes and entanglements in fishing gear. However, deaths have dipped significantly in the last two years, and the lobster industry notes that many of the entanglements have not been in lobster gear and occurred far beyond Maine, as the whales migrate up and down the Atlantic coast.

“In 2022, the Maine lobster fishery faced punitive regulations based on flawed science that would have effectively shut down the fishery,” the two senators wrote, noting the ongoing research.

“This work is ongoing, and extending the pause would allow it to continue and provide scientists and regulators with better data to inform future management decisions,” the duo continued. “It is critical that any future regulatory actions appropriately balance protecting North Atlantic right whales with the economic and practical realities facing Maine’s lobster industry.”

Alexa Dayton, executive director of the Maine Center for Coastal Fisheries, said extending the deadline for rulemaking on the whales could prove to be a “double edged sword.”

“We can track the whales now. We have a much better understanding of their patterns and where they are, and that’s informing the spatial question of where is the risk the highest,” she said.

The state and federal government have made significant investments in tracking the whales — but the federal funding provided to do that research is set to lapse in 2033, two years before the deadline that would be adopted under the new bill. It would take another appropriations rider to continue the study in parallel with any extended deadline.

Collins, who is up for reelection this year, is chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee.

“If we don’t kind of jump on the bandwagon and go with the process and kick it out four or five years, we could be sitting here five years from now with no data, more whale deaths, and a much different regime and administration that will look at the rulemaking more stringently,” Dayton said. 

“It could be a worse outcome for the lobster industry four or five years from now than if we just take it on today,” she added.

Lobstering issues don’t fall cleanly along party lines and in the House, 10 Democrats broke ranks to back Golden’s bill.

The Senate has a more comfortable GOP margin than the House and may be able to back the bill without Democratic support. However, in the House, the bill did lose two Republican votes.

“I think there’s a balance of what needs to happen. I support lobstering. I support seafood. I come from a seafood town. I’m right on the beach,” said Rep. Aaron Bean (R-Fla.), whose district includes coastline outside of Jacksonville, Fla.

“So, I just I didn’t think the bill striked the balance of where it needed to be between protecting livelihood and protecting the few whales there are,” he continued. “There’s only a handful of whales. We need to do everything we can to protect them.”

data.title: Abbott agrees to settle DOJ lawsuit over baby formula plant contamination
data.description:
Abbott Laboratories will pay $385 million to settle allegation related to how it operated a manufacturing plant tied to contaminated powdered baby formula suspected of causing infant deaths. 

Contamination led to the nation’s largest formula facility being shuttered temporarily in 2022, triggering a recall of several infant formula brands, including Similac, exacerbating existing supply chain difficulties and causing a nationwide shortage. 

The products were purchased with government funds under the Special Supplemental Nutrition Program for Women, Infants, and Children (WIC) program administered by the U.S. Department of Agriculture, which pays for more than fifty percent of all infant formula sold in the United States.   

The settlement “makes clear the safety of our children is not negotiable,” acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter said in a statement. 

The Justice Department (DOJ) had been considering criminal charges against the company, The Wall Street Journal reported, until the Trump administration closed the investigation in favor of a civil penalty.

The civil complaint from the DOJ alleges that Abbott knowingly manufactured infant formula purchased with taxpayer dollars “in an environment that put the products at unacceptable risk of microorganism contamination and significantly impacted the products’ reliability, quality, and safety.” 

The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) launched an inspection of the plant amid complaints that four infants had been hospitalized with rare bacterial infections after consuming powdered formula that was made in the facility. Two infants died from the infections. 

The inspection found unsanitary conditions and multiple strains of a bacteria that can be deadly to infants. The facility was shuttered in February 2022, and reopened in June of that year.  

The Justice Department’s complaint detailed those unsanitary conditions, including installing umbrellas to deal with roof leaks, which diverted water from production areas but created a wet environment ripe for bacterial growth. 

Similarly, the complaint alleged that Abbott “intentionally did not test for bacterial growth to avoid obtaining positive test results showing contamination,” and that in certain instances where testing demonstrated micro contamination, Abbott failed to disclose the test results when responding to requests from FDA during 2019 and 2022 inspections.

Under the settlement, Abbott didn’t admit liability or fault. The company in a statement maintained there is no evidence that its formula caused the illnesses or deaths that prompted the 2022 recall.  

The company said testing and genetic sequencing did not identify a connection between Abbott formula and the reported illnesses, which were caused by the bacterium Cronobacter sakazakii. The company also said that no unopened, distributed Abbott infant formulas have ever tested positive for Cronobacter sakazakii. 

Nearly $349 million of the Abbott settlement funds will go to the federal government and just over $36 million will go to state Medicaid and WIC programs that purchased Abbott’s formula.  

Three whistleblowers who first filed complaints about the plant will receive $69 million.

data.title: US household income breaks 58-year-old record. These groups saw the biggest gains
data.description:
(NEXSTAR) – Median household income in the U.S. has reached new heights, the Census Bureau revealed in a data drop on Tuesday.

The median household made $87,460 in 2025, the Census reported. Adjusted for inflation, that’s the highest household income since 1967.

But not everyone is feeling the gains.

Demographic data shows different groups in the U.S. felt wages grow at different paces between 2024 and 2025.

Median income rose 3% for white households, but 4.8% for Black households, the Census reports. Despite the recent gains, Black households still make far less than households on average.

There was no significant change in 2025 for Asian or Hispanic households.

For full-time workers, women saw wages grow about 3.2% in 2025. Men, however, didn’t see a boost over the one-year period.

That being said, men who are working full time still make more than women, $72,380 versus $60,760, respectively. The gap is slowly closing, the Census Bureau says, but for now women earn about 84 cents on the dollar compared to men.

There was also a difference in income growth between the country’s top earners and lowest earners. While the top 10% of households saw income go up by 1.7% to about $261,300, the bottom 10% saw a slight decline, making around $20,000 in 2025.

Looking at everyone in the U.S. together, median household income rose 2.6% in one year, or about $2,250.

Even if income is higher and inflation is lower over the past year, many Americans are still feeling worse off, consumer surveys show. A key reason is likely that inflation, even at lower levels, has been eroding income for years.

Necessities, like gas and housing, also remain particularly expensive. The national average cost of a gallon of gas is about $4.33, according to AAA.

Mortgage rates have also been rising, driving the average long-term U.S. home loan rate to its highest level in more than a year. The benchmark 30-year fixed mortgage rate rose to 6.71% in early September, mortgage buyer Freddie Mac said. Higher mortgage rates can add hundreds of dollars a month in costs for borrowers, limiting homebuyers’ purchasing power.

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

data.title: Waters has heated exchange with Bessent on AI
data.description:
Rep. Maxine Waters (D-Calif.) went after Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Tuesday for the Trump administration’s policy on artificial intelligence (AI), as warnings about the technology percolate.

During Bessent’s appearance before the House Financial Services Committee, Waters said President Trump is “blindly” pushing for the development of AI models and data centers “with absolutely no safeguards.”

The California Democrat, the panel’s ranking member, then asked Bessent whether he saw the concerns about AI from industry leaders, including Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates.

“They could stop anytime they want to,” Bessent replied, before Waters cut him off.

The 18-term lawmaker remarked, “Did you hear what your friends had to say? What the big billionaires had to say? Did you understand that they said, ‘We’re moving into a dangerous period of time. We need to watch it. We need to slow down.’ Did you hear that?” 

Leaders in the AI industry have warned about the technology’s rapid development and the implications for all facets of life. Amodei, who co-founded Anthropic with his sister in 2021, wrote in a Saturday essay that “fully addressing the risks” of AI “requires even more prudence” from companies.

“We must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models. Progress will still seem fast, and we must make wise use of the time we gain,” Amodei said.

The Anthropic CEO specifically raised concerns about AI being able to improve itself and OpenAI agents recently hacking tech startup Hugging Face, which Nvidia announced plans to purchase earlier this month.

Lawmakers on Capitol Hill have also sounded the alarm bells, with House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) urging Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) on Monday to keep the lower chamber in session to pass legislation reigning in AI. The House is set to begin a seven-week recess at the close of business on Thursday.

When Waters asked Bessent about warnings from industry leaders on AI, he said the Trump administration “has been at the forefront of examining” models. The Treasury secretary added the administration began examining top AI models “five or six months ago.”

But Waters again cut Bessent off, saying, “Your friends said watch it, be careful, that we’re moving into a dangerous time on AI. And if you don’t admit that, it means that you’re not willing to stand up to the truth.”

President Trump has dismissed the need for stronger guardrails on AI, saying Monday the “only control” the technology needs us “is a STRONG AND SMART” president. 

“There is a SICK conspiracy going on against AI and Data Centers, and the only one that is happy about it is China,” Trump wrote on Truth Social.

data.title: Massie launches effort to impeach Hegseth
data.description:
Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) on Tuesday launched an effort to impeach Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth, citing the Pentagon’s military actions against Iran. 

Massie, a frequent critic of President Trump, accused Hegseth of launching an illegal war that was not approved by Congress. He introduced articles of impeachment on the House floor against Hegseth for “high crimes and misdemeanors.”

Massie also took the remarkable step of making his resolution privileged, meaning he’s forcing it to the floor for a vote. By House rules, that vote must come within two days. 

He argued that Hegseth violated “his oath to support and defend the Constitution of the United States” and violated “his constitutional duty to take care that the laws be faithfully executed, especially with regard to the commission of war.” He added that Hegseth has “abused the powers of the Department of Defense.”

It’s not clear whether his resolution will garner GOP support. 

Massie, who lost his primary to Trump-backed Ed Gallrein in May, has previously introduced war powers resolutions to limit Trump’s military actions in Iran. 

The House, so far, has passed two war powers resolutions, with a few Republicans bucking party leadership and joining Democrats in favor of them.  Under the War Powers Resolution, a president must end unauthorized U.S. military involvement within 60 days unless Congress formally declares war or otherwise approves the operation. The president may also receive an additional 30 days to safely withdraw U.S. troops. 

Hegseth’s office did not immediately respond to The Hill’s request for comment.

In May, Hegseth traveled to Kentucky to stump for Massie’s primary opponent, former Navy SEAL Ed Gallrein. 

Hegseth ripped Massie as an obstructionist, saying that, “at some point, being against everything becomes an excuse for accomplishing nothing.” 

Gallrein beat the incumbent, ending Massie’s reelection bid. 

Updated at 1:05 p.m. EDT.

data.title: Why Democrats keep coming back to Hasan Piker
data.description:
Hasan Piker keeps saying things that should make mainstream Democrats want to keep their distance. Yet they keep coming back. Maybe that’s because he has something they need.

The socialist streamer’s latest controversy came after he warned that if American Jews continue presenting themselves as “singularly invested in Israel,” someone could eventually “take action” against them. Piker says he was warning about the danger of conflating American Jews with Israel, not making a threat or advocating violence. His remarks drew condemnation from Democrats, including politicians who have been willing to appear with him up to now.

That has led to the usual debate over whether Democrats should distance themselves from Piker. I am more interested in why they wanted to be around him in the first place.

The obvious answer is his audience. Piker reaches huge numbers of young people who aren’t necessarily watching cable news, reading newspapers or paying much attention to what politicians say on Sunday morning shows. But I don’t think his appeal can be explained by audience size alone. When politicians go on his stream, they aren’t just trying to reach his viewers. They are trying to tap into the relationship he has with them.

As a psychotherapist, I find that relationship more interesting than Piker’s politics. Think about the world as many of his younger viewers experience it. Housing feels out of reach. Dating is miserable. Democracy always seems to be in danger. The climate is approaching catastrophe. Open your phone and there’s another crisis waiting for you.

Piker gives all of this a story: Capitalism is screwing you. Billionaires are screwing you. Israel is committing atrocities. Conservatives are standing in the way of progress. Whatever the problem, there’s usually an explanation and somebody to blame.

There’s something reassuring about that. Most people don’t particularly enjoy uncertainty. It’s hard to admit that you don’t know why your life isn’t going the way you hoped, that nobody may be responsible for it, or that some problems don’t have clean solutions. It’s much easier when somebody connects the dots for you.

Anger can also feel better than anxiety. Anxiety leaves you wondering what’s going to happen and whether you can do anything about it. Anger gives all that unease somewhere to go. Instead of asking, “What am I going to do?” you get to say, “I know who did this to me.”

Still, politics doesn’t explain why someone would watch Piker for hours. He hangs out. He jokes, gets irritated, talks about politics and then wanders on to something else. He’s there day after day in a way politicians aren’t. Spend enough time watching somebody like that and you start to feel as though you know him.

That is easy to dismiss as a parasocial relationship, but dismissing it misses the point. If you’re lonely, bored, politically frustrated or just spending a lot of time online, that familiarity can matter. Piker is giving viewers a place to go.

This is also why his latest controversy may not hurt him as much as his critics expect. Imagine you’ve spent hundreds of hours watching someone and already believe much of the political establishment is dishonest or cowardly. Then the politicians and commentators you distrust tell you that the person you like has gone too far. You might reconsider him, but then you might instead conclude that he has hit a nerve.

For some viewers, the outrage becomes another reason to trust him.

This isn’t peculiar to the left. There are figures on the right whose followers respond much the same way. The difference for Democrats is that they want Piker’s audience. They know he can reach young voters they have trouble reaching themselves, which leaves them in the awkward position of criticizing him while still needing what he has built.

And what he has built isn’t easily transferred. A politician can sit across from Piker for an hour and reach his viewers, but that doesn’t mean those viewers suddenly feel about the politician the way they feel about Piker. He has spent years talking to them. He knows their language, their jokes and their grievances. They know his.

That reverses the old relationship between politicians and media personalities. It used to be the politician who conferred importance by agreeing to an interview. With someone who already commands a large and loyal audience, the calculation can run the other way. Piker doesn’t necessarily need a politician to make him relevant. The politician may need Piker to reach people who otherwise aren’t listening.

So Democrats can stop appearing with him. They can decide his latest remarks crossed a line. There may be good reasons to do both. But neither will explain why he became so influential in the first place.

Piker gives his viewers something politics often doesn’t: a way of making sense of a confusing world and a group of people with whom to make sense of it. He gives anxiety a target and frustration a culprit. And after enough hours together, he can feel less like a political commentator than somebody you know.

That’s what Democrats are trying to get close to when they go on his show. They aren’t just chasing his numbers. They’re chasing the connection behind them.

Jonathan Alpert is a psychotherapist and author of “Therapy Nation.“

data.title: Judge blocks new Trump inscription on Kennedy Center
data.description:
A federal judge on Tuesday blocked the Kennedy Center’s latest attempt to inscribe President Trump’s name back on building — and to rename the campus after him. 

U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper ruled that the Kennedy Center board cannot move forward with the plans without “Congress’s blessing,” finding that an August vote on the renaming violated his earlier injunction.

“The board resolution bucks a federal court order and a statute Congress enacted,” Cooper, an Obama appointee, wrote in a 22-page opinion.  

It is the second time that Cooper has blocked the Kennedy Center from etching Trump’s name on the front portico of the renowned performing arts center, siding with Rep. Joyce Beatty (D-Ohio), an ex-officio board member who opposes the pro-Trump plans.

In late May, Cooper ordered that Trump’s name be removed from the building’s facade, concluding that the Trump-appointed board’s decision was unlawful because only Congress had the authority to change the center’s name. 

Several attempts by the Justice Department to pause Cooper’s order were unsuccessful, and the lettering of Trump’s name was stripped in the early morning hours of June 13. It was simultaneously covered with a tarp, obscuring the change from public view. 

But the board voted on a resolution last month that it would again add Trump’s name to the facility, this time in the form of two inscriptions that read: “renovated and restored by President Donald J. Trump” and “endowed by the Trump Kennedy Center Fund.” 

The Justice Department has argued that the board is not attempting to rename the institution but rather seeking to recognize the president’s fundraising role.

Cooper’s second ruling came down just before the board was set to meet again on Tuesday afternoon decide on whether to immediately close the facility for repairs and renovations.

Developing…

data.title: NHL star Ovechkin appears in campaign video for Putin's party
data.description:
Washington Capitals star Alexander Ovechkin appeared in a political ad this week for the ruling United Russia Party, a group aligned with President Vladimir Putin.

The 40-year-old Capitals captain was spotted in the background of the video which promoted the United Russia Party ahead of Russia’s parliamentary election. He stood alongside Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov, RT editor-in-chief Margarita Simonyan and Russian military personnel.

In the video, Lavrov warned that “those who come at us with a sword, they should expect no mercy” because “when others deal with us honestly, we will always reach an agreement.”

A spokesperson for the Washington Capitals, Sergey Kocharov, told The Hill, “Alex Ovechkin is a Russian citizen who lives in Moscow with his family during the offseason and will live there following his retirement.”

“This summer, while in Russia, he was asked by his country to participate in a video campaign. As the longest-tenured athlete in Washington, D.C. and a pillar of the community, his focus and ours is on the season ahead and the continued impact he makes on the ice and in our city,” Kocharov said.

Ovechkin has been a visible supporter of Putin since 2017, even creating the “Putin Team” to support the Russian president who was up for reelection.

“Lately, in the Western Press, I’m noticing a comparison to Putin’s team. And you know, I really liked that comparison,” he wrote at the time. “Personally, I’m ready to be a member of that team. I never hid my relationship with our President, always openly supporting him.”

Ovechkin has also been outspoken about his hope for the war between Russia and Ukraine to “end soon” shortly after Moscow initiated its full-scale invasion of its neighbor in 2022.

“Please, no more war. It doesn’t matter who is in the war — Russia, Ukraine, different countries — we have to live in peace,” he told reporters.

When asked whether he supported Putin in the days following Russia’s attacks on Ukraine, Ovechkin said, “Well, he’s my president.” 

“But how I said, I’m not in politics, I’m an athlete,” he added.

Despite the answer, Putin praised Ovechkin last year when the hockey player became the top goal scorer in NHL history. 

“This achievement has become not only your personal success, but also a real celebration for fans in Russia and abroad,” Putin said in a statement.

The Russia-Ukraine conflict is ongoing, with Ukraine hitting a Russian naval base and terminal for loading oil in the past week. A Russian drone struck near a mall in northern Ukraine on Wednesday, as well, killing at least two and wounding 14 others.

The Washington Capitals posted this week that Ovechkin had returned to Washington, D.C., after the NHL’s offseason and is participating in practices for the upcoming 2026-2027 season.

data.title: DC, Maryland members seek to prevent permanent fencing at Capitol complex
data.description:
District of Columbia Del. Elanor Holmes Norton (D) and Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) announced legislation Tuesday barring permanent fencing around the Capitol, arguing the complex should remain open and accessible to the public.

The “No Fencing at the United States Capitol Complex Act” comes after the Jan. 6, 2021, attack prompted officials to erect a security fence around the grounds.

The fence remained for six months, and officials at the time considered installing a permanent barrier as part of broader security improvements.

Norton, who announced her retirement earlier this year, has long opposed permanent fencing, arguing that such a barrier would not adequately address security threats and only create more distance between Americans and their government.

“Permanent fencing would send an un-American message to the nation and the world, transforming the Capitol from a place that’s accessible to the people it serves into a fortress that locks them out,” she said in a statement. 

“The answer to security vulnerabilities is not a crude barrier that makes the Capitol look safer while doing little to address the threats,” she added.

Norton instead called for investments in intelligence, technology, training and other security measures to protect the Capitol, while preserving its accessibility.

“At a time when trust in government is at historic lows, the last thing we should do is put another physical and psychological barrier between the people and the government that serves them,” she said.

Norton also argued that the permanent fencing could affect the residential neighborhoods and disrupt businesses surrounding the Capitol.

In the months after the Jan. 6 attack, fencing and other security measures blocked streets around the complex and forced some nearby residents to take alternate routes.

“Public property should be open to the public,” Norton said.

Van Hollen, who sits on the Senate Appropriations Committee, said, “We can protect the Capitol without walling it off to the public.”

“This legislation would ensure this complex never becomes a fortress where the American people are left on the outside looking in,” the Maryland Democrat said.

data.title: Bill that could change the nickel, how you pay with cash passes through House
data.description:
(NEXSTAR) – A new penny, bound for circulation, hasn’t been minted in nearly a year. Yet the U.S. is still working to get rid of it, once and for all.

A step in that process happened Monday in the House of Representatives, where the latest version of the Common Cents Act passed by voice vote. An identical version of the bill passed in the Senate with unanimous consent last month.

The bill passed Monday varies slightly from another version of the Common Cents Act that made its way through the House and to the Senate earlier this year. While that version instructs the Treasury to stop minting the penny, it did not explicitly outline the discontinuation of a coin.

The formal end of the penny may be the chief aspect of the bill, but the Common Cents Act could also impact how you pay with cash and potentially pave the way for the U.S. to get a new nickel. Here’s what to know.

The death of the penny, sort of

The U.S. Mint stopped producing pennies last year, but it has released collectible pennies for America’s 250th anniversary.

The Common Cents Act, if enacted, wouldn’t change either of those practices. The penny would be formally sent to the bench, though one-cent coins “for sale as numismatic items” can still be produced.

As they do now, pennies would remain legal tender. The bill that most recently passed the House notes that “any one-cent coin that is minted and issued on any date before the date of the enactment of this subsection shall remain legal tender for all debts, public charges, taxes, and dues.”

It’s estimated that more than 300 billion pennies are out in the world — more than 800 pennies, or $8 worth, per U.S. citizen — trapped wherever a little Lincoln can hide.

Pay with cash? You may see change

If you’ve paid with cash within the last year or so, you may have found that retailers do not have any pennies to give you, despite how many are believed to be rolling around in the world.

Though the Common Cents Act would not help those pennies (perhaps lost in couches and collecting dust in piggy banks) get back into circulation, it would address some of the difficulties of paying with cash that have materialized.

Businesses would be allowed the option to round cash transactions to the nearest nickel. That would make a $1.82 purchase a $1.80, while $1.83 would become $1.85, for example. As simple as it sounds, some states and localities have laws prohibiting the practice. Advocates believe the Common Cents Act could iron out that confusion.

An overhaul of the nickel

With the penny handled, the Common Cents Act would also focus on the nation’s second-lowest denomination: the nickel.

The five-cent coin may have some added value as of late, especially among retailers who have had to round change on cash transactions. But it still remains extremely expensive to produce. It cost 13.31 cents to produce a single nickel in fiscal year 2025, down slightly from 13.78 cents in fiscal year 2024. Last year marked 20 consecutive years that nickel production costs remained above the coin’s face value.

One expert has even argued it would have been easier for the U.S. to ditch its nickel than the penny.

The Common Cents Act would not get rid of the nickel, but it could lead to a change in its composition. The bill allows the Treasury Secretary to test and evaluate compositions of the coin and suggest a new make-up for the nickel if it “reduces the cost” of production and “has a minimal adverse impact on machines designed to accept coins.”

That may include making the nickel out of zinc, with an outer layer of nickel. Only the penny and the $1 coin currently use zinc, which was nearly $7,000 per tonne cheaper than copper last year, the Mint reports.

Changing a coin’s composition can be difficult, though. Attempts to make the penny cheaper, for example, failed.

No changes to the nickel or how you pay with cash can take effect until the bill becomes law. And before you rush out to stock up on nickels, it’s worth noting that, according to at least one expert, that hoarding pennies may have contributed to their death. A bill that would cease the production of the nickel was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services last summer.
